summary:
SPHEREx Explorer is a web platform that transforms raw data from NASA's SPHEREx space telescope into beautiful, interactive, and analyzable images — no installation, no command line, no PhD required.

The SPHEREx mission (launched in 2025) scans the entire sky in 102 infrared wavelengths, producing an unprecedented spectral map of the cosmos. Until now, exploring this data required professional astronomy software. We made it accessible in a browser tab.
details:
SPHEREx Explorer is a browser-based web application that transforms raw infrared data from NASA's SPHEREx space telescope into interactive, colorful, and analyzable images without requiring any installation.

The backend fetches real FITS files from the official NASA/IRSA archive, removes instrumental artifacts like zodiacal light and dead pixels, and assigns colors based on the actual wavelength of each pixel. The result is a spectral painting where every stripe of color represents a different slice of the infrared spectrum.

Users can compare two observations of the same region to highlight moving asteroids or variable stars. They can also overlay known objects from NASA's JPL Small-Body Database to identify candidates for undiscovered objects.

Clicking any source estimates its color temperature through blackbody physics, presented as a friendly visual gauge. A procedural 3D model of the object is generated based on its real temperature.

A timeline slider lets users navigate between multiple observations of the same sky region, revealing how the cosmos changes across visits. The science runs under the hood, so anyone can explore the universe without prior astronomy knowledge.

- Benefits

The project brings NASA's newest space mission data to the general public, students, educators, and citizen scientists by reducing the barrier from "install astronomy software and learn to code" to simply "open a link."

For researchers, it offers fast exploratory analysis of SPHEREx data without command-line tools. For NASA, it increases public engagement with a mission that launched in 2025 and is still building its catalog.

The app provides first visualization in about fifteen seconds, with cached images loading in under two hundred milliseconds.

It maintains scientific honesty by clearly labeling classification as a candidate rather than an identification, the 3D model as an interpretation rather than a photograph, and color temperature as approximate.

It is also the first consumer-facing tool built specifically for SPHEREx data before the full sky survey is complete, which positions it as a launchpad for future features.

- Impact

In the short term, SPHEREx Explorer aims to make cutting-edge astronomy visible and understandable to non-experts. It also aims to demonstrate that NASA mission data can be a delightful browser experience rather than a technical challenge.

In the longer term, the project seeks to democratize access to astronomical data in the same way Google Earth made satellite imagery accessible to everyone.

It also aims to enable citizen science at scale once SPHEREx produces thousands of new candidate objects, and to become a resource for schools, planetariums, and science communicators worldwide.

Finally, it seeks to show space agencies that open data combined with accessible interfaces drives public engagement. The vision is to do for the invisible spectrum what Hubble did for space photography: make it beautiful, understandable, and shareable by anyone.

- Coding

The backend is written in Python 3.11 with FastAPI as the web framework. It uses astropy for FITS file handling and world coordinate system transformations, numpy and scipy for image processing, reproject for aligning observations between epochs, and Pillow for image generation.

Data access uses boto3 for NASA's public S3 archive and our Oracle Cloud mirror. Everything is containerized with Docker and deployed on Railway.

The frontend is built with TypeScript and React 18 through Vite, styled with Tailwind CSS using a custom NASA-inspired dark theme.

It features 3D visualization through Three.js with react-three-fiber and drei, zoom and pan interactions through react-zoom-pan-pinch, server state management through TanStack Query, routing through React Router v6, and icons through lucide-react. The static build is served from Railway through a lightweight Express server.

Data is stored in Oracle Cloud Infrastructure using its S3-compatible object storage. We integrate two external APIs: NASA's IRSA SPHEREx archive for raw FITS data and NASA's JPL Small-Body Database for real-time asteroid identification.

The project requires only standard development laptops with no GPU or specialized hardware, and end users need nothing more than a modern web browser.

- Creativity

The creativity of SPHEREx Explorer lies in reinterpreting invisible infrared spectral data as visual art that communicates both science and beauty simultaneously. It also lies in extracting meaningful physical information like color temperature from just two spectral bands through grounded blackbody physics, even though the dataset is limited.

Procedurally generated 3D models are built from real spectral properties rather than being decorative. The asteroid overlay turns scientific discovery into an interactive game where finding the object without a marker becomes the reward.

Technically, our spectral painting algorithm combines wavelength-based coloring with per-row normalization to reveal structure invisible in conventional astronomy software. Our lazy cloud ingestion keeps the container lightweight while scaling to hundreds of sectors, and our cache-first architecture ensures that processing happens once and is served in milliseconds afterward.

- Factors

Our team carefully considered the physical reality that SPHEREx is a spectrograph rather than a photo telescope. It uses three physically separated telescopes, each covering a different patch of sky, and a single visit yields only two spectral points per object. We designed both the user experience and the analysis to reflect these constraints honestly.

On the scientific side, we chose transparency over wow factor whenever the two conflicted. We added disclaimers about candidate classification, 3D interpretation, and color temperature degeneracy directly into the interface.

On scalability, we adopted a cache-first design where every image is hashed and stored, so a cold start happens only once per sector. We also used a lazy cloud fetch strategy that avoids bundling gigabytes into the container and keeps Railway deploys fast. Our sector-based architecture means adding a new region of the sky is a JSON entry rather than a code change.
